paras: The Wilmington City Hall mob was a crowd of thousands that surrounded the City Hall and police station of Wilmington, Delaware, on June 24, 1903, demanding the release of Arthur Corwell, the only man arrested in the burning of George White, a Black man, two nights earlier. While it waited, the crowd jeered streetcars carrying Black passengers, and according to the New-York Tribune its members dragged Black men and children from the cars and beat them. Officials released Corwell on $5,000 bail that night, after a coroner's jury found that White had been burned by persons unknown, and a magistrate dismissed the case two days later.

Corwell, a showman from Hartford City, Indiana, had been arrested on June 23 at the instance of Attorney General H. H. Ward on suspicion of taking part in the lynching. He was held for murder, "for leading the mob," in the Smyrna Times' words and at first refused bail. He said he had been at an Eagles carnival six miles away that night. A Wilmington dispatch in the Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican said a rumor that he would be brought before the coroner's inquest drew the crowd.

The crowd began gathering shortly after 7 p.m. and within an hour filled Market Street before City Hall and King Street behind the police station. Estimates ran from 7,000 (Evening Journal) to over 5,000 (Smyrna Times) and about 2,000 (Associated Press), and thirty policemen held it back.

The Evening Journal reported that every car with a Black passenger was jeered. The Tribune said Black men who came along were beaten and chased, and that mob members jumped into blocked streetcars and "assaulted colored men and children" while the police were "like dolls in the hands of the frenzied mob."

Meanwhile the coroner's jury, sitting without Corwell, heard William Carter say he had not seen Corwell assist, and found that White died "by a party or parties unknown." Officials agreed to bail, and Thomas McHugh, a wholesale liquor dealer, furnished $5,000.

When Reinhardt announced the verdict and the bail from the City Hall steps, the crowd shouted "We don't believe it" and demanded to see the prisoner. Corwell was brought out to cheers; in the Tribune's words the mob "received him from the officers' hands." Most of the crowd then dispersed, though hundreds continued to parade the streets. Later, according to the AP, about seventy-five men stoned houses of Black residents on Orange Street.

On June 25 Governor Hunn called conditions "a great humiliation to the entire State." The murder charge was to be reduced to manslaughter, which the Tribune called "a further concession to the mob sentiment." Black residents armed themselves that day, and leaders of a party of Black marchers declared they would resent the previous night's attacks, leading to further clashes.

At the June 26 hearing a workhouse warden placed Corwell at the attack on the workhouse; defense witnesses placed him at the carnival. Magistrate Hollis dismissed the case for lack of evidence "amid cheers and handclapping."

The Wilmington Evening Journal headlined "MOB SURROUNDS CITY HALL" and called the inquest "a farce" whose verdict "met with the approval of the mob." New York papers were sharper: the Tribune's headline read "MOB FREES ALLEGED LYNCHER" over "Negroes Dragged from Cars," and the Sun's read "ALL WILMINGTON IN MOB MOOD." The Associated Press version, carried in Richmond and Montgomery, called it a "Demonstration in Favor of Alleged Lyncher" that "only made much noise."

White reports kept the wire's label for White as Bishop's murderer; one dispatch said the crowd backed Corwell because it "believed or hoped" he had joined the lynching. The Black weeklies printed only wire briefs, the Wisconsin Weekly Advocate under "ARREST LYNCHERS" and the Iowa Bystander under "CORWELL IS SET AT LIBERTY," and neither described the attacks on Black people.

Accounts differ on how much violence the crowd did: the Tribune described beatings of Black men and children, the AP said the crowd "committed no overt act," and the Smyrna Times said no one was injured. On threats, the Times-Republican dispatch said "The mob made no threats," while the Smyrna Times said it was openly stated the crowd would storm City Hall at midnight.

reader.title: Wilmington City Hall mob (1903)
bases: A crowd of thousands besieged City Hall to force the release of a man held for the lynching of George White and, while gathered, jeered, chased and (per the Tribune) beat Black men and children on the streets and streetcars (A2, A4, A7, A15); no one was threatened with lynching.

No one was killed in this episode: the crowd sought to free a prisoner accused of taking part in a lynching, not to seize anyone for execution, and the Black people it attacked were beaten or roughly handled, not killed (A2, A4, A15). The lynching of George White on June 22-23 is a separate, earlier episode.

The local Evening Journal, the New-York Tribune, the AP wire and the Smyrna Times independently agree that a large crowd at City Hall demanded Corwell's release and that he was bailed and cheered (A2, A4, A8, A15); the extent of violence against Black people is disputed (A4 vs A8, A15).

accounts.label: Local paper (Evening Journal)
accounts.gist: A 'seething mass' of 7,000 held back by thirty police jeered every car with a Black passenger; Corwell was bailed after the inquest and cheered by a 'delirious throng'.

accounts.label: New-York Tribune correspondent
accounts.gist: A drinking mob dragged Black men and children from streetcars and beat them while police were helpless; judges counselled bail and the mob received Corwell from the officers.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: About 2,000 made a noisy demonstration but committed no overt act; after they dispersed, men stoned Black-occupied houses on Orange Street.

accounts.label: Delaware weekly (Smyrna Times)
accounts.gist: Over 5,000 waited two hours, with talk of a midnight attack on City Hall; several Black people were roughly handled but none injured.

accounts.label: Black weeklies (wire)
accounts.gist: Brief wire items on Corwell's arrest and his release, without the crowd's attacks on Black people.

framing.detail: The Wilmington Evening Journal headlined 'MOB SURROUNDS CITY HALL', called the inquest 'a farce' that met the mob's approval, and called White 'the negro murderer'.
The New-York Tribune headlined 'MOB FREES ALLEGED LYNCHER' with 'Negroes Dragged from Cars' and called the release the 'absolute surrender' of police to the mob.
The Sun headlined 'ALL WILMINGTON IN MOB MOOD' and 'BAILED THROUGH PUBLIC CLAMOR'.
AP papers ran 'Crowd Made Demonstration in Favor of Alleged Lyncher' and stressed that it 'only made much noise'.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate ran the arrest under 'ARREST LYNCHERS' with the wire's label for White; the Iowa Bystander ran 'CORWELL IS SET AT LIBERTY'.
